title: Something's Gotta Give
full_review:
An inveterate skirt chaser is discombobulated when, for the first time, he falls for a woman who is not half his age in the droll romantic comedy "Something's Gotta Give" (Columbia).

It's not much of a stretch for Jack Nicholson to play old dog Harry, who never met a beautiful woman under 30 he didn't pursue. This time, his impending conquest, Marin (an appealing Amanda Peet), has taken him to her Broadway playwright mom's sprawling Hamptons home for their first tryst.

Unexpectedly, however, mom Erica (Diane Keaton) and her college professor sister, Zoe (an underused Frances McDormand), also arrive. At first alarmed he's an intruder, Erica is almost as upset to learn he's a guest. How could her lovely young daughter, an auctioneer for Christie's, be dating this randy senior citizen?

Over dinner, the uneasy quartet discover Harry's a contented chauvinist, but Zoe gives him pause with a tartly delivered feminist speech. No sooner do he and Marin enter her bedroom than Harry is felled by a heart attack and rushed to the emergency room.

Handsome young Dr. Julian (Keanu Reeves, exhibiting uncharacteristic signs of life) assures all that Harry will recover but must do so nearby, where he can monitor him daily. The good doctor also makes clear he's read and admired all of Erica's plays and is romantically drawn to her.

Almost overnight, Marin and Zoe go back to their New York City jobs, leaving a very reluctant Erica to play nursemaid to Harry in her own home. Long lonely and love-starved since her divorce, she's startled to discover Harry finds her intriguing, even sexy -- although both scream in abject horror when he accidentally stumbles into her room just as she's about to get in her jammies.

Despite this, a respect and attraction begin to build, complicated by Dr. Julian's earnest courting. Having looked down on Harry as a cradle-robber, Erica now finds herself in a similar situation with Dr. Julian.

To their mutual surprise, Harry and Erica do fall in love but he succumbs to fright and flight, leaving Erica devastated -- until she recalls the pen is mightier than the sword. But can she settle for fame and fortune, and he for fun with frisky females forever?

The first thing the Catholic audience needs to be warned about is that these characters (none of whom is identified as Catholic) are all adults who feel free to embark on affairs without taking any moral considerations into account.

Given that, writer-director Nancy Meyers fashions a rather entertaining tale of the battle of the sexes taken from a middle-aged perspective. The story line itself is on the slender side, but compensating for that are the witty performances of the leads.

Keaton bares her facial wrinkles (and unfortunately, if fleetingly, everything else) in an emotional and winning portrayal that brings more depth to her role than the script would suggest. Nicholson has certainly had more challenging roles of late, yet he brings his rascally charm to Harry as he is forced to re-evaluate his cavalier lifestyle. The scenes between them are realistic and ring true, even if a few of the plot points are less than credible.

Fresh-faced Peet also shows more acting chops than previous films have allowed. In one poignant exchange with her mother, their loving relationship shines through as mother urges daughter not to settle for affairs when she should go for love and commitment.

This, of course, is the message of the movie.

Undeniably structured as an audience pleaser, viewers looking for feel-good fare will appreciate the beautiful visuals and perhaps not be bothered by the story's sentimentality and predictability. After all, as in most films, something's gotta give.

Due to a benign treatment of promiscuity, a sexual encounter, fleeting full nudity and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
